title: Introduction to the Immune System and Innate Immunity
subtitle: Recognition, barriers, cellular elimination, inflammation, and systemic defense.
author: Tikrit University · College of Medicine · Microbiology Department

blocks.text: Immunity is the integrated capacity to recognize, respond to, and eliminate infectious microorganisms, foreign substances, and other harmful agents while preserving tissue integrity and physiological homeostasis. Specialized cells, lymphoid tissues and organs, soluble mediators, and molecular recognition mechanisms continuously survey the internal environment.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Define immunity and its major functions
Distinguish innate immunity from adaptive immunity
Identify the barriers, cells, and soluble mediators of innate defense
Connect fever and acute-phase proteins to systemic defense

blocks.title: Introduction to immunity
blocks.alt: Illustration associated with immunity and host defense.
blocks.caption: Immunity protects tissues through coordinated barriers, cells, and soluble mediators.

blocks.title: Major functions of the immune system
blocks.description: Six coordinated functions preserve tissue integrity and physiological homeostasis.

items.label: Recognition
items.text: Detect potentially harmful foreign substances and microbial agents.

items.label: Tolerance
items.text: Discriminate self from non-self.
children: Maintain tolerance toward the body’s own tissues.

items.label: Elimination
items.text: Neutralize or remove infectious microorganisms and their harmful products.

items.label: Surveillance
items.text: Remove damaged, senescent, or abnormal cells.
children: Preserve tissue integrity.

items.label: Regulation
items.text: Control inflammatory responses.
children: Maintain effective defense.
Limit unnecessary tissue damage.

items.label: Memory
items.text: Retain antigen-specific experience after exposure.
children: Produce a faster and more effective response after subsequent exposure.

blocks.title: Innate and adaptive immunity
rows: Neutrophils, macrophages, NK cells, and others
blocks.description: Contrast onset, specificity, memory, cells, components, and repeated exposure.

blocks.title: Innate and adaptive immunity
blocks.caption: Innate mechanisms act rapidly; adaptive mechanisms provide antigen specificity and memory.

blocks.label: Coordinated protection
blocks.text: Protection against infectious disease depends on coordinated innate and adaptive mechanisms.

blocks.title: Age and susceptibility
rows: Placental protection is incomplete; immune immaturity increases susceptibility
Toxoplasma gondii, rubella virus, herpes viruses, and cytomegaloviruses may cross the placenta and cause congenital abnormalities, severe disease, or fetal death
Immune immaturity increases susceptibility to some infections
Measles, mumps, poliomyelitis, and chickenpox may be more severe in adults; stronger immune responses can contribute to tissue injury
Declining immune activity, physical abnormalities, and cumulative environmental exposure increase risk
Prostatic enlargement may cause urinary stasis; smoking contributes to susceptibility
blocks.description: Compare immune protection and infection risk across the major life stages.

blocks.title: Hormonal, nutritional, and stress effects
rows: Altered hormonal or enzymatic activity can increase susceptibility
Diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and adrenal dysfunction
Suppress inflammation, reduce phagocytic ingestion, and modify responses to bacterial products such as endotoxin
In diabetes: Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Candida, Aspergillus, and mucormycosis occur more frequently
Increased steroid levels are associated with greater susceptibility to some infections
Reduced C3 and factor B, interferon responses, neutrophil and phagocytic activity; leukopenia
blocks.description: Track each modifying factor, its effect on defense, and its important associations.

blocks.title: Nutritional integrity
blocks.text: Adequate nutrition supports complement, interferon responses, leukocyte numbers, neutrophil activity, and phagocytosis.

Innate immunity is present from birth, remains continuously available, recognizes broad patterns without classical antigen-specific memory, responds rapidly, and does not strengthen in the same manner after repeated exposure to the same antigen.

blocks.title: Seven mechanism groups
blocks.description: Innate protection moves from entry prevention to local elimination and systemic coordination.

items.text: Mechanical barriers and surface secretions prevent entry and remove microorganisms.
children: Skin and mucosal epithelium
Mucus, cilia, tears, saliva, urine, and intestinal movement

items.text: Antibacterial substances damage, opsonize, or inhibit microorganisms.
children: Complement
Lysozyme, lactoferrin, antimicrobial polypeptides, acids, and enzymes

items.text: Microbial antagonism prevents pathogen colonization.
children: Competition for nutrients and space
Antimicrobial products and prevention of attachment

items.text: Cellular factors engulf or kill microbial and abnormal targets.
children: Neutrophils, monocytes, and macrophages
Natural killer cells

items.text: Inflammation recruits defense components to injured tissue.
Fever coordinates a systemic response to infection or inflammation.
Acute-phase proteins increase systemic resistance, limit tissue injury, and promote repair.

blocks.title: Skin and mucosal protection
blocks.description: Each exposed surface combines mechanical clearance with chemical or biological protection.

items.label: Skin and conjunctival epithelium
items.text: Intact epithelium blocks microbial entry.
children: Burns, trauma, and surgery increase infection risk.
Sebaceous fatty acids and normal flora inhibit many bacteria and fungi.

items.label: Mucous membranes
items.text: Physical and chemical defenses protect the mouth, respiratory tract, and genitourinary tract.
children: Mucus traps organisms and lubricates surfaces.
Ciliary movement, cellular shedding, and tight junctions support clearance.
Antibacterial substances, antibodies, and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue provide additional protection.

items.label: Oral cavity
items.text: Continuous salivary flow removes microorganisms.
children: Lysozyme damages susceptible bacterial cell walls.
Antibodies and resident microbial products support mucosal protection.
Swallowed material enters gastrointestinal defenses.

items.label: Stomach and small intestine
items.text: Acidity, enzymes, bile, and movement restrict ingested organisms.
children: Low gastric pH and proteolytic enzymes destroy many microorganisms.
Bile salts disrupt bacterial membranes.
Rapid intestinal movement reduces microbial attachment.

items.label: Intestinal microbiota
items.text: Rich resident flora in the ileum and large intestine provides colonization resistance.

items.label: Upper respiratory tract
items.text: Nasal architecture and hairs filter large particles.
children: Sticky mucus traps inhaled particles and microorganisms.
Cilia transport trapped material toward the pharynx.
Coughing removes material.
Mucopolysaccharides interact with influenza and certain other viruses.

items.label: Genitourinary tract
items.text: Flow and local chemistry restrict ascending infection.
children: Urine flushes microorganisms.
Spermine and zinc in semen have antibacterial activity.
Adult vaginal acidity is unfavorable to many pathogens.
The cervical mucus plug forms a physical barrier.

items.label: Conjunctiva and tears
items.text: Continuous tear secretion washes the ocular surface.
children: Lysozyme, lactoferrin, and secretory IgA provide antimicrobial protection.
Reduced or absent tear secretion increases ocular infection risk.

blocks.title: Lysozyme
blocks.text: Alexander Fleming described lysozyme in 1922. This low-molecular-weight muramidase hydrolyzes peptidoglycan. Tear concentrations act mainly against selected bacteria, particularly Gram-positive organisms; higher concentrations inside phagocytes contribute to broader intracellular killing.

blocks.title: Antibacterial substances in blood and tissues
rows: Membrane disruption, opsonization, and inflammatory promotion
Relatively heat-stable activity against Bacillus anthracis and related bacilli
Basic antimicrobial polypeptides derived from leukocytes and associated with platelets
Creates conditions unfavorable for growth in muscle and inflammatory sites
Generates reactive antimicrobial products in milk
blocks.description: Connect each soluble innate-defense factor to its principal action or setting.

blocks.title: Microbial antagonism
rows: E. coli produces colicin in the large intestine
Resident organisms compete for nutrients and space
Microbiota reduces pathogen access to epithelial binding sites
Antibiotic disruption can permit opportunistic proliferation and disease
blocks.description: Reduce colonization resistance to its core mechanisms and consequences.

blocks.text: Neutrophils, monocytes, and macrophages ingest and destroy microorganisms, foreign particles, and cellular debris.

blocks.title: Phagocytic destruction
blocks.description: Follow a microorganism from surface contact to intracellular degradation.

steps.title: Attachment
steps.description: A microorganism or foreign particle adheres to the phagocyte surface.

steps.title: Ingestion
steps.description: The membrane encloses the target through an endocytic process.

steps.title: Phagosome
steps.description: The ingested target occupies an intracellular vesicle.

steps.title: Lysosomal fusion
steps.description: The phagosome fuses with a lysosome.

steps.title: Phagolysosome
steps.description: Oxygen radicals, digestive enzymes, and other degradative mechanisms destroy the target.

steps.title: Degradation
steps.description: Microbial material and debris are broken down.

blocks.title: Phagocytosis
blocks.alt: Diagram showing engulfment and intracellular destruction by a phagocyte.
blocks.caption: Attachment and ingestion form a phagosome; lysosomal fusion forms a phagolysosome for degradation.

blocks.title: Clinical limits and evidence
rows: Resist intracellular digestion and may multiply within phagocytes, allowing dissemination
Loss of granulocytes increases infection susceptibility
Defective intracellular killing demonstrates the importance of phagocyte function
blocks.description: Distinguish microbial survival strategies from disorders that reveal the importance of phagocytes.

blocks.title: Natural killer cells
blocks.text: NK cells recognize abnormal host cells and directly kill virus-infected and malignant cells. Interferons enhance NK-cell activation and cytotoxicity during early defense.

steps.title: Vasodilation
steps.description: Increased blood flow delivers plasma proteins, neutrophils, and other phagocytes.

steps.title: Increased vascular permeability
steps.description: Protein-rich exudate containing immunoglobulins and complement enters tissue.

steps.title: Leukocyte emigration
steps.description: Leukocytes pass through endothelial gaps into injured tissue.

steps.title: Chemotaxis
steps.description: Neutrophils and macrophages follow mediator gradients.

steps.title: Phagocytosis
steps.description: Recruited cells attach, engulf, and destroy microorganisms with oxygen radicals and digestive enzymes.

blocks.title: Fever
rows: Gram-negative endotoxin; staphylococcal enterotoxin; group A streptococcal erythrogenic toxin
IL-1, interferon-alpha, and IL-6; macrophages produce IL-1
Activates leukocytes; restricts bacterial growth by decreasing iron availability; enhances antibody production and T-cell proliferation; protects host cells against some TNF-alpha effects
blocks.description: Review pyrogen categories and the beneficial effects of fever.

blocks.title: Acute-phase proteins
rows: Rapidly rises during infection or injury and can activate complement
Enhance resistance, limit tissue injury, and promote repair
blocks.description: Link the major acute-phase proteins to their contributions during infection and tissue injury.

blocks.title: Integrated innate response heading
blocks.alt: Embedded graphic from the integrated innate-response sequence.
blocks.caption: Innate defense proceeds from entry prevention to adaptive activation.

steps.title: Remove microorganisms
steps.description: Mucus, cilia, tears, saliva, urine, intestinal motility, and coughing

steps.title: Inhibit growth
steps.description: Gastric acid, bile, lysozyme, lactoferrin, antimicrobial peptides, and normal microbiota

steps.title: Eliminate
steps.description: Neutrophils, monocytes, and macrophages perform phagocytosis

steps.title: Resolve and repair
steps.description: Remove microorganisms and damaged tissue, then restore homeostasis

blocks.title: Complementary defense levels
rows: Skin and mucosal epithelium prevent entry
Mucus, cilia, tears, saliva, urine, intestinal motility, and coughing remove microbes
Acidity, bile, lysozyme, lactoferrin, peptides, complement, and interferons inhibit or destroy
Vascular change, leukocyte recruitment, and chemotaxis concentrate defense
Fever and acute-phase proteins coordinate whole-body defense
blocks.description: Use the defense levels as a final visual memory sheet for innate immunity.

exam.title: Introduction and innate immunity exam
exam.instructions: Answer every question. Submit once to receive a score, correct answers, and explanations.

questions.prompt: Which feature belongs to innate immunity?
questions.explanation: Innate immunity responds rapidly through broad recognition.
Resident microbiota competes with pathogens and inhibits attachment.
Lysozyme is a muramidase that attacks peptidoglycan.

questions.prompt: How many major mechanism groups of innate immunity are listed?
questions.explanation: The groups are barriers, antibacterial substances, microbial antagonism, cellular factors, inflammation, fever, and acute-phase proteins.

questions.prompt: Match each defense to its action.
questions.explanation: Each mechanism contributes a distinct layer of defense.

questions.history: A patient receives prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics and then develops overgrowth by an opportunistic organism.
questions.prompt: Which protective mechanism was most directly disrupted?
questions.explanation: Antibiotics can disrupt resident microbiota and colonization resistance.

questions.prompt: What immediately follows ingestion during phagocytosis?
questions.explanation: Engulfment encloses the target in a phagosome.

questions.prompt: Fusion of a phagosome with a lysosome forms a _____.
questions.explanation: The fused degradative compartment is the phagolysosome.

questions.prompt: Which organisms may resist intracellular digestion within phagocytes?
questions.explanation: Mycobacteria and Brucella can survive and multiply intracellularly.

questions.prompt: Match inflammatory events to their effects.
questions.explanation: These events recruit soluble and cellular defenses.

questions.history: A patient with absent tear secretion develops recurrent ocular infection.
questions.prompt: Which lost combination best explains the risk?
options: Mechanical washing plus lysozyme, lactoferrin, and sIgA
questions.explanation: Tears provide continuous clearance and complementary antimicrobial factors.
IL-1 is produced by macrophages and participates in fever.

questions.prompt: How many stages are listed in the integrated innate response from entry prevention through adaptive activation?
questions.explanation: The integrated sequence contains eight stages.

questions.prompt: The acidic environment that inhibits many pathogens is found in the adult _____.
questions.explanation: Adult vaginal acidity is a genitourinary defense.

questions.history: An older man has urinary stasis caused by prostatic enlargement and develops recurrent urinary infection.
questions.explanation: Urinary stasis is an age-associated physical risk factor.

questions.prompt: Match antimicrobial substances to their settings.

pairs.right: E. coli in the large intestine

questions.explanation: Each item has a specific setting or example.

questions.prompt: Which finding is associated with protein-calorie malnutrition?
questions.explanation: Malnutrition can reduce complement, interferon responses, neutrophil and phagocytic activity, and leukocyte numbers.

questions.history: A child has chronic granulomatous disease and recurrent infections.
questions.prompt: Which process is most directly impaired?
questions.explanation: The condition demonstrates the importance of phagocyte microbial killing.
